newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ASIA METALS- TRADE DOUBTS CHINA COPPER STOCK MOVES.
newsitem.headline: ASIA METALS- TRADE DOUBTS CHINA COPPER STOCK MOVES.

text.p: Asian dealers said on Friday they were a sceptical of an analyst's report which indicated a substantial portion of the large rise in London Metal Exchange (LME) copper stocks in July came from Chinese state reserves.

U.K.-based Bloomsbury Minerals Economics said in a quarterly report on Thursday, a large chunk of the 106,625-tonne increase in inventories last month came from the return of copper from China's Strategic Reserve Bureau (SRB) to LME warehouses.
"I believe that quite a bit of material came from China, but whether the bulk of the movement is from the SRB is open to question," a senior copper trader said.
"It could be partially true," another dealer said. "I don't think the amounts were in the order mentioned by the report. I'm a bit sceptical about it."
A senior dealer for a foreign metal house in Singapore said there was no sign "that a deal of that magnitude was done."
"Information leaks like a sieve. We haven't got a sense that happened," he said, adding some copper was delivered to LME warehouses from China but not in substantial quantities.
One dealer said two big European houses delivered copper "to take advantage of the backwardation in the market" and that South Korean metal houses also moved metal to the LME.
"I don't believe the Europeans were moving material for the Chinese or the Chinese were moving it through them," he said. "I also heard that the Koreans moved a lot of material to the LME."
The volume of copper in LME warehouses reached 245,775 tonnes on Thursday, up from 143,750 tonnes at the end of April.
The LME's Singapore warehouse, the nearest exchange store to China, held 62,050 tonnes of copper on warrant on Thursday against the 16,200 tonnes reported at end-April.

In the aluminium market, cash premiums around Asia have come under pressure due to the flaring backwardation on the LME following a speculative squeeze centred on August dates and linked to short options positions.
The cash/threes ballooned on Thursday to about $20 from $5/10 on the previous day and was last indicated at $14/$16.
"Aluminium premiums may come under pressure as the back (backwardation) widens because this would make it more expensive to carry the metal," a trader said.
Dealers said premiums for western 20-25 kg ingots in Singapore eased to $80-$95 a tonne from $85-$95 previously.
Aluminium premiumj were quoted at between $80-$85 a tonne CIF Japanese ports against last week's $85-$90.
"The very best I heard in Japan was $84. But a range of $80-$85 seems reasonable," one dealer said.
In Korea, spot aluminium premiums were seen at $85-$90 a tonne CIF Pusan against last week's $90-$95.
Premiums in Taiwan dipped to about $85 a tonne CIF Keelung and Kaoshiung from the previous week's $85-$90. They were seen at $95-$100 a tonne CIF Hong Kong against $100 last week.
In Indonesia, they dipped to about $95-$100 a tonne CIF Jakarta against last week's $100.
"The increase in the backwardation is causing a bit of concern. Premiums are a little bit under pressure now," one dealer said.

The base metal trade could not immediately confirm a report that China's Zhuzhou smelter, caught short on the wrong end of a recent squeeze on the LME zinc market, will delay August zinc shipments to users and traders in Taiwan.
One zinc dealer said the report seems unlikely.
"If anything, the metal houses there seems to have ample zinc. We have not heard of any delays by Zhuzhou," he said.
